title: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We take White and open e4, Black meets e5.
The knight develops to f3.
Black develops to c6. We're playing the Four Knights Scotch — a great opening for improving players: it brings every piece out on sound principles, not gimmicks.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black completes the knights with ...Nf6.
Now the point: d4, opening the centre — and dangerous if Black plays inaccurately.
Black takes and we recapture with the knight.
Black develops the bishop to c5.
The most principled move is the bishop to e3 — it defends our knight and sets a threat: take on c6, and Black's bishop on c5 falls because the queen behind it hangs.
Black releases the tension with ...Bxd4 — already an inaccuracy, conceding the centre.
We recapture with the bishop, and now we hold the two bishops and a bigger share of the centre.
Black castles. Our priority: finish developing quickly while preserving the bishop pair.
We keep the pair by retreating the bishop to e3 — the aggressive c5 would just invite ...d6; on an open board we want both bishops.

Black plays ...h6 — and that's a hook. A good moment to train your castling intuition: I'd castle queenside, because ...h6 invites g4–g5 to prise it open, and with the bishop pair and more centre, an opposite-side race favours us.
We begin with the flexible queen to d2.
Black tucks the king to h7.
We castle queenside. Note f3 isn't only to stop ...Ng4 — it also props up e4 and prepares g4.
Black plays d6.
We play f3 — unlike h3, it supports the e4-pawn, so it's automatic here: the English-Attack setup of f3, g4 and h4.
Black develops the bishop to e6.
The king to b1 is a fine improving move, but Black has so little counterplay that we simply start the attack with g4.

Black centralises with the knight to e5 — a good move, and now attacking calls for creativity. We must defend f3 — losing it collapses our kingside — while helping the attack, and the queen to g2 does both, landing on the g-file beside the rook to bear down on g7. Then g5 rolls in. And the Shankland question returns: can we play f5 anyway? Yes — f5 traps and wins the queen, and even after a capture the pin from the bishop to d3 decides. The theme throughout: keep asking "what if I do it anyway" instead of recoiling from a threat.

One more: keep the tension. Against the bishop to e3 the main move is ...Bb6, retreating to a defended square — not ...d5, which blunders a piece to the x-ray, nor the passive ...d6. Learn to spot an undefended piece sitting on an x-ray.
